HEEWON STYLE — a KOREAN WEBTOON movie still PAINTED like a premium digital painting, the look of a dramatic manhwa cover. A 2:1 movie frame composed for a 2:1 letterbox crop (nothing important at the top or bottom edge). The shot the scene names (wide establishing, two-shot, close-up, over-the-shoulder) from a dramatic camera angle (low three-quarter, worm's-eye, high overhead or dutch), never a flat straight-on catalogue pose. Named characters' FACES are drawn exactly like the attached character sheet: the same confident ink linework drawn BOLD and THICK with real line weight — a heavy tapered black contour around the whole silhouette and the hair mass, medium lines for folds and features, fine lines only for lashes and loose strands and manhwa face design (eye shape, brows, nose, jaw, hairline and hair), recognisably those characters, in the clothes the scene gives them. EVERYTHING ELSE IS PAINTED: visible textured brushwork — loose digital-paint strokes and dry-brush, charcoal-like hatching that follow every fold of the silk and every plate of armour, the shadows built from layered strokes, the brightest ridges laid in with single confident strokes, a faint paper-and-canvas grain; at the edges of the garments the linework breaks into loose sketchy strokes. NOT flat cel-shading, NOT smooth airbrushed gradients, NOT a clean vector look, NOT photoreal, NOT 3D. Night on the Tang flagship, low over-the-shoulder: the Black Tortoise’s armoured shoulder and grey beard as a dark blurred mass at the left edge. Right third, sharp: Yung in a crimson Tang officer’s robe and black futou cap at the high rail beside one hanging iron lantern that lights the side of his face and his knuckles on the rail; his eyes on the black sea, the face giving nothing away. The rail runs out into an enormous dark sea; on the far horizon a faint string of red lanterns. PLACE (match the attached pl_white_river board and the battle map): the wide grey-brown mouth of the White River, low blue hills on both banks, tidal mudflats, shifting sandbars and reed beds. The Tang fleet of 170 dark tower-ships and warships lies anchored in ONE tight line across the narrow throat of the river, bows to the sea; the Yamato and Baekje boats come in from the open sea to the south-west, hundreds of small open rowing boats packed together. Alongside, a Tang deck stands a man’s height above any Yamato boat; the Tang broadside is a wooden wall the Yamato boats break on. BANNERS BY SIDE: vermilion Tang banners fly ONLY on the dark Tang hulls; red Wa sunburst banners ONLY on the Yamato boats; Tang sails are plain deep red, no emblem; the Tang sun disc holds an abstract black smudge, never a readable character. REFERENCE SHEET. TOP ROW, left to right: LEFT face = liurengui, SECOND face = yung. Copy each face exactly; give each person the dress the scene names. SMALLER SECOND ROW, left to right: ship_tang (copy its exact shape), place board pl_white_river (keep this exact architecture and ground). BLACK TORTOISE — Look: Tang general of sixty-two: lean and upright, long narrow face, deep-set patient eyes, long grey moustache and a long thin grey beard to the chest, grey hair under a black Tang futou cap (or a Tang helm in battle). Dress: Tang general's round-collared robe in dark slate-green over Tang mingguang armour: two round polished chest discs, lamellar skirt, shoulder guards; a vermilion cloak; a long brush-and-tablet case at the belt. Tang palette: vermilion, black, steel. Colour #3d4a48. PRINCE YUNG — Now: In Tang service: same face (high topknot, thin moustache, small chin beard); a Tang officer's round-collared robe (panling) in deep crimson with a black leather belt, black futou cap tied at the back over the topknot, black boots. No Baekje gold scrollwork, no jougwan. He looks like a Tang officer who was born somewhere else. Colour #d4b45a. PLACE White River (백강 (금강 하구)) — attached board /pl_white_river.png; keep this exact architecture and ground. Kingdom banners: copy field colour and emblem from the attached flag_*.png ref onto period silk war-banners — tall poles behind each side, long streamers, small pennants on spear-tips and saddle-backs. Painted silk, wind-whipped, torn and smoke-stained in battle; never a flat modern flag graphic. Each side's banner colour is the clearest colour on its half of the frame, so the kingdom reads at a glance. Tang banners: vermilion silk with a yellow sun disc and a dark brush glyph inside it — painted as an illegible brush mark, never readable text. Attached flag /flag_tang.png. Baekje banners: warm yellow silk with a darker gold door-lintel and three gold stars. Attached flag /flag_baekje.png. SHIPS: copy the attached ship board for each kingdom exactly (hull shape, mast count, sail colour and battens) and keep that same ship in every still of the scene. Boards are design only: ignore their bright daylight sky and calm sea, repaint the ship in the scene light. 7th-century timber ships only, never European hulls, cannon or funnels. TRUE SCALE (real 7th-century measures; a man is 1.65 m): ships are drawn life-size against their crews and against each other, never toy boats with giant men. A man standing on deck is about 1/15 the length of a 24 m warship and 1/20 of a 35 m tower-ship; a deck bulwark reaches his chest; the waterline is two men's height below a warship deck. Dozens of men fit along one side of a warship, each one small against the hull, masts four or five men tall. When two kingdoms' ships share a frame, keep their real length ratio. Tang louchuan tower-ship: huge dark timber hull with a multi-storey deck castle, two or three masts of deep red battened sails, the largest ship on any sea. Size: the flagship tower-ship is about 35 m long and 8–9 m wide, deck about 3 m above the water, its three-storey castle rising about 12 m (seven men tall), up to two hundred men aboard; the ordinary Tang warship is about 24 m long with forty to ninety men, its deck a man's height higher than any Yamato or Baekje boat. Its broadside looks like a city wall. BACKGROUND AND LIGHT (painterly tenebrism): the background IS the place and the moment of the scene — open sky if they are in the sky, the hall if they are in a hall, the gate, the river, the snow — painted loosely in atmospheric brushwork (drifting smoke, cloud, haze, mist, falling snow, embers) in the scene's own colours, soft and out of focus, with a faint bokeh of small lights; it has colour, weather and depth — never a flat black void, never a detailed set; crowds and armies only as massed painted shapes dissolving into haze. ONE hard directional key light that belongs to the place (a brazier, a lamp, the sun through cloud, a torch, moonlight) rakes across the faces and clothes from the side or from below, modelling them in high contrast with deep painted shadows and a thin edge of the same light along the silhouette. Each character's colour lives in that light and in the atmosphere around them — never a glow aura or halo. Faces and bodies act the beat: real expressions, real weight, mid-motion. Faces from the sheet; new poses, never the sheet's stance. Each named person appears once, never cloned. Everyone wears period clothing of their own court (Korean, Tang, Yamato, Mohe furs), never European dress. No text, no speech bubbles, no panel borders, no watermark. NIGHT GROUND: the frame is built on BLACK — crushed ink-black night masses around the subject, the place pulled out of the dark only where the one key light (fire, lamp, torch, moon) falls, small warm bokeh in the black; the figure is the bright thing in a dark frame.
